implementation_notes: In JavaScript the micro-optimisation that matters is usually not arithmetic at all - it is shape stability and allocation. The dominant cliffs are a megamorphic property access (an object with many different hidden classes at one call site, which defeats the inline cache) and an allocation in a hot loop (which triggers GC and, in Node, costs far more than the work). The profiling tools are the V8 CPU profiler (--prof plus --prof-process), Chrome DevTools Performance panel with allocation sampling, and Node's --cpu-prof; --trace-gc shows the garbage-collection pauses that are usually the real cost. So the micro-optimisation that pays is: make objects the same shape, hoist property lookups, avoid allocation in the loop, and use a typed array for numeric data. Inlining is the JIT's job and there is no manual control; the developer-facing lever is monomorphism, exactly as this catalog's inline-functions record notes.
idiom_name: V8 --prof / Chrome Performance with allocation sampling, applied at the measured hotspot; shape stability and allocation are the usual wins
pitfalls: Measuring CPU time while ignoring GC: in Node the garbage-collection pauses are often the real cost, and --trace-gc is how you see them.
Objects with different construction order have different hidden classes, making the access site polymorphic or megamorphic and defeating the inline cache.
A property access (obj.x) inside a hot loop is a lookup; hoisting it to a local is the cheapest win and is measurable.
A micro-benchmark of a hot function does not reflect the steady state, because the JIT optimises after the function becomes hot - a one-shot call measures the interpreter.
for...in and property enumeration are slow and hidden-class dependent; use a typed array or an explicit index loop for numeric data.
